question.stem: A café delivers meals from two branches, A and B. The café refunds the cost of any delivery that takes more than 40 minutes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
In one week, 60 meals were delivered from branch A. The table shows the cumulative frequency of the delivery times, $t$ minutes, for these 60 deliveries. All of these deliveries took more than 10 minutes.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Delivery time } (t \text{ minutes}) & t \le 20 & t \le 30 & t \le 40 & t \le 50 & t \le 60 \\ \hline \text{Cumulative frequency} & 6 & 26 & 51 & 58 & 60 \\ \hline \end{array}$
parts.answer: (i) 31.5 minutes  (ii) 9.28 minutes  (iii) 90% of 60 is 54 deliveries; the table shows 51 deliveries within 40 minutes and 58 within 50 minutes, so the number within 45 minutes is not known (anywhere from 51 to 58) and the claim cannot be checked.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Calculate an estimate of the mean delivery time from branch A.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation of the delivery times from branch A.

subparts.label: (iii)
subparts.text: The café advertises that 90% of its deliveries arrive within 45 minutes. Explain why the table cannot be used to decide whether this is true for branch A.
subparts.answer: 90% of 60 $= 54$ deliveries. The table gives 51 deliveries within 40 minutes and 58 within 50 minutes, so the number of deliveries within 45 minutes could be anything from 51 to 58; whether it reaches 54 cannot be decided from the table.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In the same week, 60 meals were delivered from branch B. The table shows some information about these delivery times, in minutes.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Minimum} & \text{Lower quartile} & \text{Median} & \text{Upper quartile} & \text{Maximum} \\ \hline 12 & 20 & 26 & 42 & 58 \\ \hline \end{array}$
The mean delivery time from branch B is 29.6 minutes. Devi says that, because this mean is smaller than the mean delivery time from branch A, fewer deliveries from branch B were refunded than from branch A. Explain why Devi is wrong.
parts.answer: Branch A: $60 - 51 = 9$ deliveries took more than 40 minutes, so 9 were refunded. Branch B: the upper quartile is 42 minutes, so at least $\frac{1}{4} \times 60 = 15$ deliveries took 42 minutes or more, all of which took more than 40 minutes and were refunded. At least 15 is more than 9, so branch B refunded more deliveries; a smaller mean does not show how many long deliveries there were.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Two of the 60 deliveries from branch A are chosen at random. Find the probability that both of these deliveries were refunded.

question.answer: (a)(i) 31.5 minutes  (a)(ii) 9.28 minutes  (a)(iii) 90% of 60 = 54; the table gives 51 within 40 min and 58 within 50 min, so the count within 45 min is unknown  (b)(i) A refunded 9; B's upper quartile 42 > 40 means at least 15 refunded, so B refunded more  (b)(ii) $\frac{9}{60} \times \frac{8}{59} = \frac{6}{295}$
question.solution:
(a)(i) The table is cumulative, so the class frequencies must be recovered first. Since every delivery took more than 10 minutes, the classes are $10 < t \le 20$, $20 < t \le 30$, $30 < t \le 40$, $40 < t \le 50$, $50 < t \le 60$ with frequencies
$6, \; 26 - 6 = 20, \; 51 - 26 = 25, \; 58 - 51 = 7, \; 60 - 58 = 2$ (total 60).
Mid-values $x$: $15, 25, 35, 45, 55$.
$\sum fx = 6(15) + 20(25) + 25(35) + 7(45) + 2(55) = 90 + 500 + 875 + 315 + 110 = 1890$.
Estimated mean $= \frac{1890}{60} = 31.5$ minutes.
Marks: M1 for the frequencies $6, 20, 25, 7, 2$ (or $\sum fx = 1890$ seen); A1 for $31.5$. Setter's check on the trap: using the cumulative frequencies as if they were frequencies gives $\frac{6(15) + 26(25) + 51(35) + 58(45) + 60(55)}{201} = \frac{8435}{201} = 42.0$, a plausible-looking wrong answer; dividing that numerator by 60 gives 140.6, which exceeds the largest possible time.

(a)(ii) $\sum fx^2 = 6(15^2) + 20(25^2) + 25(35^2) + 7(45^2) + 2(55^2) = 1350 + 12500 + 30625 + 14175 + 6050 = 64700$.
Standard deviation $= \sqrt{\frac{64700}{60} - 31.5^2} = \sqrt{1078.33\ldots - 992.25} = \sqrt{86.083\ldots} = 9.2781\ldots = 9.28$ minutes (3 s.f.).
Check by deviations: $\sum f(x - 31.5)^2 = 6(272.25) + 20(42.25) + 25(12.25) + 7(182.25) + 2(552.25) = 5165$, and $\sqrt{5165 \div 60} = 9.28$.
Marks: B1 for $9.28$ (follow-through from wrong frequencies in (i) allowed if the method is correct).

(a)(iii) 90% of 60 $= 54$ deliveries. The table shows 51 deliveries within 40 minutes and 58 within 50 minutes, so the number within 45 minutes is somewhere from 51 to 58. It may or may not be 54 or more, so the claim cannot be confirmed or rejected from the table. (The 54th delivery lies inside the class $40 < t \le 50$ and the table gives no information about where inside a class the times lie.)
Marks: B1 for a statement that identifies 54 (or 90% of 60) and that 45 minutes lies inside a class whose split is unknown (51 within 40 minutes, 58 within 50 minutes). A generic "the data is grouped" without these figures earns nothing.

(b) Devi's premise is true ($29.6 < 31.5$, from (a)(i)) but does not decide the question: the mean is an average of all the times and says nothing about how many individual deliveries were long.
Branch A: the number of deliveries taking more than 40 minutes is $60 - 51 = 9$, so branch A refunded 9 deliveries. (This is exact, because 40 minutes is a class boundary.)
Branch B: the upper quartile is 42 minutes, so one quarter of the 60 deliveries, that is $\frac{1}{4} \times 60 = 15$ deliveries, took 42 minutes or more. Every one of these took more than 40 minutes, so branch B refunded at least 15 deliveries (possibly more, since some deliveries between 40 and 42 minutes may also exist).
At least 15 is more than 9, so branch B refunded more deliveries than branch A, not fewer.
Marks: B1 for 9 refunds at branch A; B1 for "at least 15" at branch B from the upper quartile (the quartile must be the reason, not the maximum of 58 alone).

(c) The refunded deliveries from branch A are those with $t > 40$: $60 - 51 = 9$ of the 60 (found in (b), or read afresh from the table). The two deliveries are chosen from the 60 without replacement, so
$\text{P(both refunded)} = \frac{9}{60} \times \frac{8}{59} = \frac{72}{3540} = \frac{6}{295} = 0.0203$ (3 s.f.).
Marks: M1 for $\frac{9}{60} \times \frac{8}{59}$ (the 9 must come from $60 - 51$ and the second factor must be $\frac{8}{59}$); A1 for $\frac{6}{295}$ or $0.0203$. Setter's check on the traps: treating the draws as with replacement gives $\left(\frac{9}{60}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{400} = 0.0225$, tidy but wrong; using the 51 deliveries that were NOT refunded gives $\frac{51}{60} \times \frac{50}{59} = \frac{85}{118}$.

Setter's data check for branch B: the summary statistics given are those of an actual set of 60 times (for example $12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 17, 17, 18, 18, 19, 19, 19, 20, 20, 21, 21, 22, 22, 23, 23, 23, 24, 24, 24, 25, 25, 25, 26, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 36, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 42, 42, 42, 42, 43, 43, 44, 44, 45, 45, 46, 46, 46, 46, 58$): minimum 12, lower quartile 20, median 26, upper quartile 42, maximum 58, sum 1776 so mean 29.6, and 17 deliveries exceeded 40 minutes, consistent with the "at least 15" argument.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Data handling and analysis: reading a cumulative frequency table and recovering class frequencies; estimating the mean and the standard deviation of grouped data using class mid-values (calculator statistics mode permitted); the meaning of a percentage of a data set and of the upper quartile (a quarter of the data at or above it); reasoning about a summary statistic in context. 4052 Probability: combined events, two selections without replacement, by multiplying probabilities (no tree diagram needed). No cumulative frequency curve has to be drawn or read, no interpolation inside a class is required (part (a)(iii) is precisely that it cannot be done), nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: The 2024/2025 statistics questions give either a frequency table to be processed (GCE 2024 P2 Q7: apples, then a histogram and a three-draw probability) or a cumulative frequency curve and a box plot to be read off (GCE 2025 P2 Q2: quiz times; GCE 2023 P1 Q8: heights), and GCE 2024 P1 Q21 hides an unknown in a list. None presents a cumulative frequency TABLE from which the class frequencies must first be recovered before the mean and standard deviation can be estimated, and none sets one real threshold (the 40-minute refund) against two differently summarised groups so that the candidate must see that a class boundary gives an exact count for one branch while a quartile gives only a lower bound for the other, and that the mean answers neither. The single probability part is a two-draw without-replacement product whose first step is to read the refund count off the cumulative table, not a three-draw ordering count as in GCE 2024 P2 Q7(b)(iii) or GCE 2025 P2 Q7(c)(ii). The context (meal deliveries from two branches, a refund rule and an advertised 90%-within-45-minutes claim) appears nowhere in the corpus or in this paper, whose other contexts are a resold bicycle, a treadmill on hire purchase, two banks, a nature-reserve map and a band's ages; there is no median calculation and no tree diagram. Numbers are new throughout and the threshold values (40 on a class boundary, 45 inside a class, an upper quartile of 42 just above 40) were chosen so that each reasoning part turns on one specific fact, and the probability's with-replacement wrong answer (9/400) is as tidy as the right one.

answers.(a)(ii): Standard deviation = sqrt(64700/60 - 31.5^2) = sqrt(86.0833...) = 9.28 minutes (3 s.f.)
answers.(a)(iii): The table gives cumulative frequencies only at the 10-minute boundaries, so the number of deliveries taking 45 minutes or less is not known - it could only be estimated by assuming the 7 deliveries between 40 and 50 minutes are spread evenly, which need not be true.
answers.(b)(i): The number of refunds depends on how many deliveries took more than 40 minutes, not on the mean: for branch B the upper quartile is 42, so at least 15 of the 60 deliveries took more than 40 minutes, whereas for branch A only 60 - 51 = 9 did, so branch B in fact had more refunds.

issues: Part (b)(ii) asks about deliveries from branch A, but it is placed under part (b), which is otherwise entirely about branch B - it reads as a mislabelled part that belongs under (a). The part is still answerable as printed (9 of A's 60 deliveries exceeded 40 minutes).

In (a)(ii) the question does not state whether the population or sample standard deviation is wanted; the population value 9.28 is given (the sample value would be 9.36). At O-Level the population value is the expected answer.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.note: Both recover the class frequencies 6, 20, 25, 7, 2 from the cumulative table (first class 10 < t <= 20 from 'more than 10 minutes'); sum fx = 1890, mean 31.5 min. Re-derived.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.note: sum fx^2 = 64700; 64700/60 - 31.5^2 = 86.083; SD = 9.28 min (3 s.f.). Re-derived. The examiner's population-vs-sample remark is not an issue: the population formula is the O-Level convention and both sides give 9.28 (the sample value 9.36 is not what 4052 expects).

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.note: Same fact on both sides: 45 minutes lies inside the class 40 < t <= 50, so the count within 45 minutes is anywhere from 51 to 58 and whether it reaches 90% of 60 = 54 cannot be decided. The examiner's wording (the 7 deliveries in that class need not be spread evenly) is the same reason; the setter's scheme rightly demands the 51/58 (or 54) figures rather than a generic 'the data is grouped'.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.note: Identical argument: branch A refunded exactly 60 - 51 = 9 (40 is a class boundary); branch B's upper quartile of 42 puts the 46th to 60th ordered times at or above 42 > 40, so at least 15 refunds; 15 > 9, so Devi's conclusion is wrong and the mean cannot settle it. Checked the setter's illustrative data set of 60 times: min 12, LQ 20, median 26, UQ 42, max 58, sum 1776 (mean 29.6), 17 over 40 minutes, so the five figures and the mean are jointly attainable.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.note: Both: 9 refunded of 60, drawn without replacement, 9/60 x 8/59 = 72/3540 = 6/295 = 0.0203 (3 s.f.). Re-derived. The examiner's placement remark is a labelling point, not a key point: the part is unambiguous as printed.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement anywhere; all five values and both explanation arguments re-derive independently, the round-1 fixes (the two-draw probability on branch A's refunds in place of the prose comparison; the standard-deviation sentence removed from the (b) stem) were applied exactly as named, and the blind examiner's two remarks are a part label and the population-SD convention, neither of which touches the key.
fixes: Relabel (b)(ii) as a separate part (c) [2] with the same wording ('Two of the 60 deliveries from branch A are chosen at random. Find the probability that both of these deliveries were refunded.'), so (b) stays 'In the same week, 60 meals were delivered from branch B ...' with (b) [2] as the Devi part alone. The placement under (b) does not read naturally: in every real paper a sub-part sits inside the data set its preamble introduces (GCE 2024 P2 Q7(b)(iii) is on the 150 tomatoes of the (b) histogram; GCE 2025 P2 Q7(c)(ii) on the full-time workers of the (c) table), and (b)(i)'s comparison of the two branches does not turn a branch-A probability into a branch-B sub-part. As (c) it follows the comparison naturally (the refund count 9 is on the page, the refund rule is in the question's opening stem) and the marks stay 4 + 2 + 2. The part cannot be moved to branch B, since a five-figure summary gives only 'at least 15' refunds, never an exact count.
verdict.why: AT the 2024/25 standard: the cumulative table hides the one decision in (a)(i) (a candidate who treats the cumulative figures as frequencies gets a tidy-looking 42.0), (a)(ii) is the routine 1-mark SD as in GCE 2024 P2 Q7(a)(iii), each explain part turns on one specific fact (45 sits inside a class; the upper quartile fixes at least 15 refunds, so a generic 'the mean does not show spread' earns nothing) as GCE 2024 P2 Q7(b)(i) does, and the two-draw probability is the routine that follows the refund count, all finishable in about 12 minutes; the mark split (3 prose of 8, one probability part) now matches the real statistics questions. Not a re-skin: delivery times with a refund threshold, a cumulative table and a five-figure summary share only the genre with the apples/tomatoes and quiz-times questions (gates pass, nearest GCE 2024 P2 Q7 at Jaccard 0.045). The one light edit is the part label.

question.stem: The diagram shows the cross-section of a road tunnel. The curved roof $ATB$ of the tunnel is an arc of a circle, centre $O$ and radius $r$ metres. The road surface $AB$ is horizontal and $AB = 6$ m. $T$ is the highest point of the tunnel, $TO$ is vertical and $T$ is $4.5$ m above the road.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $r = 3.25$.
parts.answer: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$: $OM = 4.5 - r$, $AM = 3$, so $r^2 = (4.5 - r)^2 + 3^2$, giving $9r = 29.25$ and $r = 3.25$ (shown).

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Calculate the length of the arc $ATB$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Calculate the area of the cross-section of the tunnel.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: A double-decker bus is $2.5$ m wide and $4.4$ m high. The bus is driven through the tunnel along the centre of the road. Determine whether the bus can pass through the tunnel. Show your working.
parts.answer: No. At $1.25$ m from the centre of the road the roof is only $1.25 + \sqrt{3.25^2 - 1.25^2} = 4.25$ m above the road, and $4.25 < 4.4$, so the top corners of the bus would hit the roof (equivalently, at a height of $4.4$ m the tunnel is only $1.6$ m wide).

question.answer: (a) $r = 3.25$ shown from $(4.5 - r)^2 + 3^2 = r^2$; (b)(i) $12.8$ m; (b)(ii) $24.5$ m$^2$; (c) No — the roof is $4.25$ m high at $1.25$ m from the centre line, less than $4.4$ m.
question.figure_description: The cross-section of the tunnel, drawn approximately to scale with 1 m = 1 unit. Take the circle of radius 3.25 with centre O at (0, 1.25), but draw ONLY the part of the circle on or above the line y = 0: a single solid arc starting at A (-3, 0) on the left, rising over T (0, 4.5) at the top and coming down to B (3, 0) on the right — this is the major arc. Do NOT draw the part of the circle below y = 0. Draw the chord AB as a solid horizontal line (the road surface). Mark O as a small dot labelled O (it sits above the road, on the vertical line through T). Do NOT draw the radii OA or OB and do not print the letter r anywhere. Draw a dashed vertical line from T down through O to the midpoint of AB; beside it place a dimension arrow from the road up to T labelled 4.5 m. Below AB place a dimension arrow labelled 6 m. Label A and B at the two ends of the chord and T at the top of the arc. Print NOTHING else: no value 3.25, no 1.25, no angle sizes in degrees or radians, no arc length, no area, no bus, no shading, and do not label the midpoint of AB.
question.solution:
(a) Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Then $AM = 3$ m, and $O$, $M$ and $T$ lie on the vertical line through $T$. Since $OT = r$ and $MT = 4.5$, $OM = 4.5 - r$.
In right-angled triangle $OMA$: $OA^2 = OM^2 + AM^2$
$r^2 = (4.5 - r)^2 + 3^2$
$r^2 = 20.25 - 9r + r^2 + 9$
$9r = 29.25$
$r = 3.25$ (shown)

(b)(i) $OM = 4.5 - 3.25 = 1.25$ m.
In triangle $OMA$, $\cos \angle AOM = \frac{1.25}{3.25} = \frac{5}{13}$, so $\angle AOM = 1.1760$ rad.
$\angle AOB = 2 \times 1.1760 = 2.3520$ rad.
The arc $ATB$ goes over the top of the tunnel, so it is the major arc: reflex $\angle AOB = 2\pi - 2.3520 = 3.9312$ rad.
Arc $ATB = r\theta = 3.25 \times 3.9312 = 12.776 = 12.8$ m (3 s.f.).
[In degrees: $\angle AOM = 67.38^\circ$, reflex $\angle AOB = 225.24^\circ$, arc $= \frac{225.24}{360} \times 2\pi \times 3.25 = 12.8$ m.]

(b)(ii) The cross-section is the major segment, so
Area $=$ major sector $OATB$ $+$ triangle $OAB$
$= \frac{1}{2}(3.25)^2(3.9312) + \frac{1}{2}(6)(1.25)$
$= 20.762 + 3.75$
$= 24.512 = 24.5$ m$^2$ (3 s.f.).
[Alternatively: circle $-$ minor segment $= \pi(3.25)^2 - \frac{1}{2}(3.25)^2(2.3520 - \sin 2.3520) = 33.183 - 8.671 = 24.5$ m$^2$.]

(c) The bus is $2.5$ m wide, so its top corners are $1.25$ m from the centre line of the road, i.e. $1.25$ m horizontally from the line $OT$.
Height of the roof at that horizontal distance $= OM + \sqrt{3.25^2 - 1.25^2} = 1.25 + \sqrt{9} = 4.25$ m.
Since $4.25 < 4.4$, the top corners of the bus would hit the roof. The bus cannot pass through the tunnel, even though the tunnel is $4.5$ m high at the centre.
[Equivalently: at a height of $4.4$ m, which is $3.15$ m above $O$, the tunnel is $2\sqrt{3.25^2 - 3.15^2} = 2\sqrt{0.64} = 1.6$ m wide, and $1.6 < 2.5$.]
question.syllabus_check: 4052 only: Pythagoras' theorem in a right-angled triangle with an unknown radius (a); cosine ratio in a right-angled triangle giving an angle, reflex angle, arc length $s = r\theta$ with the angle in radians — the degree route $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$ is equally acceptable (b)(i); area of a major segment as reflex sector $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ plus triangle, or circle minus minor segment (b)(ii); Pythagoras again for the clearance at a given horizontal distance (c). No circle-property theorems are needed (the half-chord follows from the vertical line of symmetry $TO$), no calculus, no identities, no surds beyond $\sqrt{9}$ and $\sqrt{0.64}$. Answers: $r$ exact; $12.8$ m and $24.5$ m$^2$ to 3 s.f.; (c) decided by $4.25 < 4.4$.
question.originality_note: New situation and structure: a road tunnel whose cross-section is the MAJOR segment of a circle (the road is a chord below the centre), with the radius hidden behind the chord and the height, then a vehicle-clearance decision that turns on the bus's top corner rather than its centre line. Nothing in GCE 2024 P2 (Q8: congruent triangles from two equal chords, a major arc from a GIVEN 1.8 rad, two intersecting circles with a sine-rule angle) or GCE 2025 P2 (Q6: quadrilateral with three given radian angles, sine and cosine rule, then a pyramid) involves a segment cross-section, a radius to be found from chord-and-sagitta, or a clearance test; the exemplars (sector-to-cone net, wiper area, sector perimeter from a given angle, cyclic quadrilateral angles) share neither the configuration nor the sequence of parts. Numbers are the 5-12-13 triangle scaled by 0.25, so every intermediate is clean while the naive centre-only check in (c) still produces a tidy but wrong 'yes'. Does not repeat this paper's Q5 (incircle of a triangle), Q6 (coordinate geometry) or Q9 (rainwater mensuration).

answers.(a): shown — with O at height h above AB, T is (h + r) above the road so h = 4.5 - r; the perpendicular from O to the chord AB bisects it, so 3^2 + h^2 = r^2 giving 9 + (4.5 - r)^2 = r^2, i.e. 9 + 20.25 - 9r = 0, 9r = 29.25, r = 3.25 (so O is 1.25 m above the road)
answers.(b)(i): 12.8 m (arc ATB = 12.7763... m; cos(AOT-half angle) = 1.25/3.25 so angle AOB = 2.35201 rad = 134.760 deg, reflex angle AOB = 3.93117 rad = 225.240 deg, arc = 3.25 x 3.93117)
answers.(c): No, the bus cannot pass through. Along the centre of the road the bus occupies 1.25 m each side of the centre line; at a horizontal distance of 1.25 m from the centre the height of the tunnel is 1.25 + sqrt(3.25^2 - 1.25^2) = 1.25 + 3 = 4.25 m, which is less than the bus height of 4.4 m.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both show r = 3.25 by the same route: the perpendicular from O bisects the chord (AM = 3), OM = 4.5 - r, and r^2 = (4.5 - r)^2 + 9 gives 9r = 29.25. Re-derived; O is 1.25 m above the road, so the section is a major segment and O lies inside it as the figure shows.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.note: Both give 12.8 m: cos AOM = 1.25/3.25 = 5/13, angle AOB = 2.3520 rad, reflex angle AOB = 2pi - 2.3520 = 3.9312 rad, arc = 3.25 x 3.9312 = 12.776 m. Re-derived. The 5-12-13 triangle OMA (1.25, 3, 3.25) keeps the numbers clean.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.note: Both give 24.5 m^2 as major sector + triangle: (1/2)(3.25^2)(3.9312) + (1/2)(6)(1.25) = 20.761 + 3.75 = 24.51. Re-derived, and the alternative circle - minor segment (33.183 - 8.671) agrees.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both: no. The bus's top corners are 1.25 m from the centre line, where the roof is 1.25 + sqrt(3.25^2 - 1.25^2) = 1.25 + 3 = 4.25 m above the road, and 4.25 < 4.4. Re-derived; equivalently at 4.4 m (3.15 m above O) the tunnel is 2 sqrt(3.25^2 - 3.15^2) = 1.6 m wide. The trap works: comparing the bus height with the 4.5 m centre height gives a tidy-looking 'yes'.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement anywhere; setter and blind examiner match on all four parts and every value re-derives independently (r = 3.25, arc 12.8 m, area 24.5 m^2, roof 4.25 m at the bus's corner so the bus cannot pass).
fixes: Stem precision: 'The cross-section is part of a circle, centre O and radius r metres' describes a region as part of a curve. Write it as a real paper would: 'The curved roof ATB of the tunnel is an arc of a circle, centre O and radius r metres.' (keep 'The road surface AB is horizontal and AB = 6 m. T is the highest point of the tunnel, TO is vertical and T is 4.5 m above the road.').

(c) verb: 'Explain, with working, whether the bus can pass through the tunnel' is not a GCE imperative; use 'Determine whether the bus can pass through the tunnel. Show your working.' (the GCE 2025 P2 Q9(c) 'justify with calculations whether' shape).

Figure: drop the dashed radii OA and OB (keep the dot at O, the dashed vertical TO to the road and the two dimensions 6 m and 4.5 m; r is named in the stem, so the label on OB is not needed). With OA drawn, triangle OMA is handed to the candidate in (a) and the triangle OAB in (b)(ii); without them the candidate chooses the triangle for the Pythagoras step and the sector-plus-triangle decomposition, which is the 'chosen, not named' step the 2024/25 checklist asks for. The figure as described prints no value the candidate must find, which is correct.
verdict.why: AT the 2024/25 standard: (a) [3] is a show-that placed where it gates every later part and worth its marks, the candidate forming OM = 4.5 - r with no 'form an equation' cue (the GCE 2025 P1 Q20(b) shape); (b)(i) [3] hands the candidate the major-arc decision (reflex angle in radians, as GCE 2024 P2 Q8(a)(ii) but with the angle to be found first); (b)(ii) [2] makes the candidate choose the decomposition of a major segment; (c) [2] is a context that changes the maths (the corner at 1.25 m, not the centre height) with a tidy wrong answer for the wrong decision, and the whole runs about 14 minutes. Radians, arc length, sector and segment areas are all 4052. Not a re-skin: a single-circle tunnel section with the radius to be found is neither the chord-congruence/two-circle GCE 2024 P2 Q8 nor any 2025 P2 question (gates pass, nearest GCE 2015 P1 Q19 at Jaccard 0.06). The three edits are register and figure polish, none touches the key or the weight.

question.stem:
A school collects rainwater from the roof of its garden shed and uses it to water the garden. The information below is used to plan the system.

Collecting rainwater
Volume of rainwater collected, in litres $= 0.8 \times$ area of roof in m$^2$ $\times$ rainfall in mm.
$1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres.
The roof of the shed has an area of $36$ m$^2$.

Water tanks available
$\begin{array}{|c|l|l|} \hline \text{Tank} & \text{Shape} & \text{Dimensions} \\ \hline A & \text{Cylinder} & \text{diameter } 1.2 \text{ m, height } 1.5 \text{ m} \\ \hline B & \text{Cylinder} & \text{diameter } 1.4 \text{ m, height } 1.6 \text{ m} \\ \hline C & \text{Cuboid} & 1.5 \text{ m long, } 1.0 \text{ m wide, } 1.8 \text{ m high} \\ \hline \end{array}$
The tank must stand upright, with the whole of its bottom resting on the rectangular concrete base beside the shed. The concrete base measures $1.6$ m by $1.3$ m.

Watering the garden
The garden is watered once a day by a drip line connected to the tank. The drip line delivers $2.5$ litres of water per minute and runs for $24$ minutes each day. On a day when the temperature rises above $32^\circ$C, the drip line runs for a further $12$ minutes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the capacity of Tank A is $1700$ litres, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In a trial, Tank A is connected to the roof of the shed. One evening the tank is one-quarter full. During the night, heavy rain fills the tank and $320$ litres of water overflows. Calculate the rainfall, in mm, that night.
Give your answer correct to the nearest millimetre.
parts.answer: $55$ mm (from $55.38\ldots$ carrying $1700$ litres, or $55.3$ carrying $1696.46$ litres)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The school expects a dry spell of $28$ days with no rain, including $8$ days when the temperature rises above $32^\circ$C. The tank will be full at the start of the dry spell and must supply all the water for the garden until the dry spell ends. The school wants to buy the tank with the smallest capacity that can do this and can stand on the concrete base. Suggest which tank the school should buy. Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.answer: Tank C. Water needed $= 20 \times 60 + 8 \times 90 = 1920$ litres. Tank A holds only $1700 < 1920$ litres. Tank B holds $\pi \times 0.7^2 \times 1.6 = 2.46$ m$^3 = 2460$ litres, enough, but its diameter $1.4$ m is greater than the $1.3$ m width of the base, so it cannot stand on the base. Tank C holds $1.5 \times 1.0 \times 1.8 = 2.7$ m$^3 = 2700 \ge 1920$ litres and its $1.5$ m by $1.0$ m bottom fits on the $1.6$ m by $1.3$ m base.

question.answer: (a) $\pi \times 0.6^2 \times 1.5 = 1.696\ldots$ m$^3 = 1700$ litres (3 s.f.)  (b) $55.4$ mm  (c) Tank C: need $1920$ litres; A holds $1700 < 1920$; B holds $2460$ but diameter $1.4$ m $> 1.3$ m base width; C holds $2700 \ge 1920$ and fits
question.solution:
(a) Radius of Tank A $= \frac{1.2}{2} = 0.6$ m.
Capacity $= \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 0.6^2 \times 1.5 = 0.54\pi = 1.6964\ldots$ m$^3$.
$1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres, so capacity $= 1696.46\ldots$ litres $= 1700$ litres, correct to 3 significant figures. (Shown.)
[Equivalently in cm: $\pi \times 60^2 \times 150 = 1\,696\,460$ cm$^3 = 1696.46$ litres.] Marks: M1 for $\pi \times 0.6^2 \times 1.5$ (radius $0.6$, not $1.2$), A1 for $1696.46\ldots$ converted to litres and rounded to $1700$.

(b) The tank is one-quarter full, so the water needed to fill it is $\frac{3}{4} \times 1700 = 1275$ litres.
The rain also produces $320$ litres of overflow, so the volume collected that night is $1275 + 320 = 1595$ litres.
Volume collected $= 0.8 \times 36 \times$ rainfall, so $28.8 \times$ rainfall $= 1595$.
Rainfall $= \frac{1595}{28.8} = 55.38\ldots = 55$ mm, correct to the nearest millimetre.
[Carrying $1696.46$ litres instead of $1700$ gives $\frac{1272.35 + 320}{28.8} = 55.3\ldots$, also $55$ mm.] Marks: M1 for $\frac{3}{4} \times 1700 + 320 = 1595$ (the volume collected is the space in the tank plus the overflow), A1 for $55$ mm.

(c) Water used on an ordinary day $= 2.5 \times 24 = 60$ litres.
Water used on a day above $32^\circ$C $= 2.5 \times (24 + 12) = 2.5 \times 36 = 90$ litres.
Water needed for the dry spell $= 20 \times 60 + 8 \times 90 = 1200 + 720 = 1920$ litres.
Tank A: capacity $1700$ litres $< 1920$ litres, so Tank A runs dry before the dry spell ends. Not suitable. [The trap: ignoring the $8$ hotter days gives $28 \times 60 = 1680 \le 1700$ and wrongly accepts Tank A.]
Tank B: capacity $= \pi \times 0.7^2 \times 1.6 = 0.784\pi = 2.463\ldots$ m$^3 = 2460$ litres $\ge 1920$ litres, so it holds enough water. But a cylinder of diameter $1.4$ m needs a base at least $1.4$ m wide in every direction, and the concrete base is only $1.3$ m wide ($1.4 > 1.3$, even though $1.4 < 1.6$). So Tank B cannot stand on the base. Not suitable.
Tank C: capacity $= 1.5 \times 1.0 \times 1.8 = 2.7$ m$^3 = 2700$ litres $\ge 1920$ litres, so it holds enough water. Its bottom is $1.5$ m by $1.0$ m, and $1.5 \le 1.6$, $1.0 \le 1.3$, so it stands on the base.
Tank C is the only tank that meets both requirements, so the school should buy Tank C.
Marks: M1 for $90$ litres on a day above $32^\circ$C (rate $\times$ time with the extra $12$ minutes), A1 for $1920$ litres, M1 for the capacity of Tank B ($\pi \times 0.7^2 \times 1.6 = 2460$ litres), B1 for rejecting Tank B on the base ($1.4$ m $> 1.3$ m), B1 for Tank C with $2700 \ge 1920$ and the $1.5$ m by $1.0$ m fit, A1 for rejecting Tank A ($1700 < 1920$) and stating Tank C.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Problems in real-world contexts: reading an information sheet (a formula, a table of tank sizes, a rate) and making and justifying a decision with working. Mensuration: volume of a cylinder ($\pi r^2 h$, radius from a stated diameter) and of a cuboid; conversion m$^3 \to$ litres from the sheet's $1$ m$^3 = 1000$ litres. Rate: litres per minute $\times$ minutes, a total over a number of days. Nothing outside 4052: no money, no percentages, no similarity, no calculus. Precision: (a) states 3 s.f. because it is a show-that; (b) and (c) fall under the paper's rubric (answers in whole litres and mm to 3 s.f.). Marks: 2 + 2 + 6 = 10, about 15 minutes at 1.5 minutes per mark: (a) one routine, (b) one accounting step then a reversed formula, (c) a demand calculation with one rule to apply, then three tank checks of which two are decisions that change the outcome.
question.originality_note: A new situation: sizing a rainwater tank for a school garden. No money and no percentages anywhere (the paper already spent both in Q2 and in P1). GCE 2024 P2 Q9 (candles: mass from a volume formula, a wax/oil split, similar cylinders, buying packs, pricing) shares only the word 'cylinder'; there is no similarity, no pack choice and no price here. GCE 2025 P2 Q9 (an electric-car road trip: a distance table, charging rates, a time budget and a cost claim) shares nothing: no journey, no speed, no time budget, no claims to test. The GCE 2023 specimen Q9 (exercise minutes and calories), GCE 2021 P2 Q10 (bridge-cable masses against a limit) and GCE 2020 P2 Q10 (a year of living costs in pounds) are different situations and different chains. The 2024/25 standard is met by what the candidate must decide: in (b) that the water collected equals the empty space plus the overflow, then a reversed formula; in (c) that the dry-spell demand must include the hotter days' extra running time (without it $1680 \le 1700$ and Tank A wrongly passes), and that a cylinder's diameter must fit the SHORTER side of the base (Tank B fits the $1.6$ m length but not the $1.3$ m width, and it has enough capacity, so only the geometric check rejects it). Both decisions change the answer; the wrong path gives a tidy-looking Tank A. The final 6-mark part is a 'Suggest ... Justify' decision after two short warm-ups, the shape the last question has kept every year.

answers.(c): Tank C. Water needed = 28 x 2.5 x 24 + 8 x 2.5 x 12 = 1680 + 240 = 1920 litres. Tank A holds 1696 litres (< 1920) — too small. Tank B holds pi(0.7)^2(1.6) = 2463 litres (enough) but its 1.4 m diameter will not fit on the 1.6 m by 1.3 m base (needs 1.4 m in both directions, base is only 1.3 m wide). Tank C holds 1.5 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 2.7 m^3 = 2700 litres >= 1920 litres and its 1.5 m by 1.0 m base fits on the 1.6 m by 1.3 m concrete base. So buy Tank C.

issues: (b) is mildly rounding-sensitive: using the unrounded capacity 1696.46 litres gives 55.3 mm, while a candidate who uses the 1700 litres established in (a) gets 55.4 mm. A mark scheme should accept both.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both show 1700 litres. Re-worked: radius 0.6 m from the 1.2 m diameter, pi x 0.6^2 x 1.5 = 0.54 pi = 1.69646 m^3 = 1696.46 litres = 1700 litres to 3 s.f. The target is true and the two steps (radius from diameter with pi r^2 h; m^3 to litres then round) carry M1 A1 exactly as the key says.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Setter 55.4 mm carrying the shown 1700 (3/4 x 1700 + 320 = 1595; 1595 / 28.8 = 55.38), blind 55.3 mm carrying the exact 1696.46 (1272.35 + 320 = 1592.35; / 28.8 = 55.29). Same model (collected = the three-quarters of the tank still empty + the overflow), same reversed formula; the 0.09 mm gap is only which capacity is carried, and both are correct. The key already accepts 55.3 in a parenthetical; the scheme must carry both as printed answers.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give Tank C by the same route. Re-worked: 2.5 x 24 = 60 and 2.5 x 36 = 90 litres a day; 20 x 60 + 8 x 90 = 1920 litres. A: 1696.46 < 1920, runs dry. B: pi x 0.7^2 x 1.6 = 0.784 pi = 2.463 m^3 = 2460 litres holds enough, but a 1.4 m diameter needs 1.4 m across the 1.3 m width of the base, so it cannot stand (the stem's 'whole of its bottom resting on' closes any overhang reading). C: 1.5 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 2.7 m^3 = 2700 litres and 1.5 by 1.0 fits 1.6 by 1.3. Both wrong paths land tidily: 28 x 60 = 1680 <= 1700 accepts A; checking B only against the 1.6 m length or by area (1.54 < 2.08) accepts B, and 'smallest capacity' then picks B over C. The key is right.

verdict.key_verdict: No substantive disagreement: the 55.3 / 55.4 split in (b) is the carried capacity (exact 1696.46 versus the shown 1700), both are correct and the key must accept both; every other answer, and the two traps in (c), are confirmed by my own working.
fixes: accept 55.3 or 55.4 in (b): print the key's answer as '55.4 mm or 55.3 mm (55.4 carrying the shown 1700 litres, 55.3 carrying 1696.46 litres)' so the mark scheme carries both as full-credit answers rather than a parenthetical. Cleaner still, in the examination's own style: add 'Give your answer correct to the nearest millimetre.' to (b), which makes both routes give 55 mm and removes the rounding fork altogether.

(c) mark scheme, light: three marks for the demand (M1 60 and 90, M1 the sum, A1 1920) is heavy and Tank B's fresh cylinder volume earns nothing. Reallocate one mark per decision or fresh computation, the way SEAB's justify schemes fall: M1 90 litres on a hot day (the extra 12 minutes), A1 1920 litres, M1 Tank B capacity 2460 litres, B1 B rejected on 1.4 m > 1.3 m, B1 C with 2700 >= 1920 and the 1.5 by 1.0 fit, A1 A rejected (1700 < 1920) and Tank C stated.
verdict.why: AT the 2024/25 standard for 10 marks and the last question's kept shape (two 2-mark warm-ups, then one 6-mark 'suggest and justify'): (b) makes the candidate build the model (collected = the empty three-quarters of the tank + the overflow) and reverse the sheet's formula, and (c) hands over two decisions that each change the answer with a tidy wrong result on the other path (the hot days' extra 30 litres, without which 1680 <= 1700 accepts A; a cylinder must clear the SHORTER side of the base, without which B, the smaller of the two that hold enough, is bought), with the rest routine and the whole finishable in about 12 of the 15 minutes; gates passed (nearest corpus item GCE 2017 P2 Q8 at jaccard 0.019), and it is neither the candle costing of GCE 2024 P2 Q9 nor the EV journey of GCE 2025 P2 Q9 in situation or chain. A 4 not a 5 because (b) forks at 3 s.f. on which capacity is carried, which real papers avoid, and (c) sits at the lighter end of the 2024/25 final part (no running state to track as in GCE 2025 P2 Q9(c)).
